contributions.headingText: Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) is a stromal myofibroblastic proliferation lining anastomosing slit-like spaces.

Fascicular (cellular) pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia; atypical pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia [[Hoda SA, Brogi E, Koerner FC, et al., editors. Rosen’s breast pathology. 4th ed. Philadelphia (PA): Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2014.]]

PASH can occur in both sexes and commonly presents as an incidental finding, although it can be associated with other benign or malignant lesions. Palpable mass-forming PASH (so-called nodular PASH or PASH tumour) presents as a painless, unilateral, firm or rubbery mass. In rare instances, PASH can present as rapid diffuse enlargement of both breasts. When visible on mammography, PASH occurs as a mass or focal asymmetry without calcifications; by sonography it appears as a hypoechoic mass and by MRI as either a postcontrast well-delineated mass or an area of non-mass enhancement {26949063}. In males, PASH most often occurs as a palpable mass or nodule and is usually associated with gynaecomastia {9659260; 7544764}. PASH with stromal giant cells, in the background of gynaecomastia, may be associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 {11407482}. PASH can occur in accessory breast tissue along the milk line {16096415}.
PASH is most commonly seen in women with a mean age in the fourth to sixth decades of life, but it can also occur in postmenopausal women, in men, and in children {19606909; 22583194}.

In premenopausal females and prepubertal boys, PASH is driven by hormonal imbalances. PASH is believed to be an aberrant response of myofibroblasts to endogenous or exogenous hormones – most likely progesterone, because the staining intensity of PR is greater than that of ER {1989462; 20586640}.
PASH does not have characteristic molecular features.

When mass-forming, PASH occurs as a well-circumscribed, unencapsulated, firm rubbery mass of 1–12 cm in size {7872425}, and in some cases it has a multinodular appearance. The cut surface is tan-white and homogeneous.

PASH is a proliferation of myofibroblasts intermixed with terminal duct lobular units. The stroma is composed of dense collagen with anastomosing, slit-like channels, devoid of red blood cells and lined by spindle cells, which can resemble flattened endothelial cells. The spindle cells most often have bland cytology and lack mitotic activity or atypia. PASH is present as the stromal component of gynaecomastia (in particular florid gynaecomastia), and peri–terminal duct lobular unit oedema and gynaecomastoid-type changes in ductal epithelium are also present. PASH may also be seen in the stroma of fibroadenomas and phyllodes tumours.

The term “fascicular PASH” refers to the formation of cellular bundles of myofibroblasts arranged in a fascicular pattern {7872425} lacking slit-like spaces and merging with conventional PASH. Fascicular PASH can mimic myofibroblastoma, but it is differentiated by the presence of typical breast epithelial elements within the borders of the tumour. Rarely, PASH may contain atypical spindle cells with nuclear enlargement and hyperchromasia (atypical PASH), and there is one documented case in the literature in which sarcoma arose from PASH {18611932}. Rarely, PASH can show cytoplasmic inclusions similar to those observed in digital fibromas {28676174}.

The stromal cells of PASH show positive immunohistochemical staining for CD34, actin, desmin, and hormone receptors, with PR staining observed more frequently than ER staining {7872425; 1989462}. The stromal cells of PASH are negative for endothelial markers (CD31, ERG, D2-40), cytokeratins, and S100.

PASH must be distinguished from angiosarcoma and other vascular lesions. True blood-filled anastomosing vascular channels lined by malignant endothelial cells are the key feature of angiosarcoma.

Essential: bland spindle cell myofibroblasts; an anastomosing network of slit-like channels; dense acellular collagenous stroma.

Desirable: immunohistochemistry negative for endothelial markers if needed; scattered acini and ducts in the background.

PASH need not be excised when identified in a core biopsy, provided there is histological–imaging concordance. Although local recurrences of PASH have been reported, it is unclear whether excised PASH has truly recurred or whether new PASH foci have arisen in a hormone-rich environment {20708765}. The clinical implications of atypical PASH are unknown.
